title: Offline Reinforcement Learning in MQL5: Conservative Q-Learning from Historical Trade Logs Without Live Exploration
text:
Introduction
Most reinforcement learning approaches to trading assume the agent can interact with the market during training — it tries an action, observes a reward, and updates. That's reasonable in a simulator; dangerous on a live account, since "trying an action" means a real order with real slippage while the policy is still bad at its job. Training offline removes that risk, but not the risk of deploying a bad policy once training is done: a frozen policy can still trade badly, it just can't make things worse by continuing to experiment.
This article works through a different setup: training a trading policy entirely from a fixed batch of historical transitions, with no further market interaction during training. The dataset is whatever a rule-based strategy, a manual trader, or a prior EA already logged — states, the action taken, the reward realized, and the state that followed. The policy learns from that log alone, then deploys frozen: no exploration, no live trial-and-error, no chance for learning itself to cause money loss.
Offline training also matters for auditability: a fixed dataset can be scrutinized and replayed before any order is placed, with every transition inspectable in a spreadsheet — worth the trade for a desk that has to explain its systems to a risk committee, even though an online agent's exploration policy keeps changing. This article doesn't demonstrate formal dataset versioning, a seed/parameter log, or an explicit train/test split, though — call it replayable rather than fully audited.
The catch: naive Q-learning on a fixed dataset doesn't work well out of the box. If the logged data never tried going long during a certain volatility regime, a standard Q-network will still happily assign that action a high value, because nothing in the data ever pushed the estimate back down. The bootstrapped Bellman update propagates these overestimates to state-action pairs never observed, and at deployment the policy may exploit them — extrapolation error, the central problem offline RL has to solve.
Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) adds a penalty term that pushes down the Q-values of actions the current policy would pick broadly, while leaving room for actions actually present in the data to fit the true return — the network stays conservative where evidence is thin, trusting its own estimates only where data backs them up. CQL's literature frames this as a lower bound on the true value. With a single network and 838 transitions, treat "conservative" as accurate and "lower bound" as motivating theory, not guarantee.
Scope note:
this article implements CQL natively in MQL5, with no ONNX model and no external ML framework — the training script, network, and deployment EA are all plain
.mq5
/
.mqh
files. A Python companion script only converts MQL5's own CSV exports into the transition format the training script reads; it never touches the model itself.

Why offline RL needs a conservative correction
Picture a dataset from a trend-following strategy that almost never shorted during low-volatility mornings, since its own rules kept it flat then. Standard Q-learning still computes a Q-value for "short" in that regime — the network must output something for every action, even ones barely touched — and because training bootstraps from the reward plus the best next action's discounted value, an accidental overestimate there gets treated as ground truth, propagating backward through every earlier state that could reach it. Nothing proves it wrong offline.
Q-learning's update target is
r + gamma * max_a' Q(s', a')
— the network bootstraps from its own estimate of the best next action, not a true observed outcome. Online, a wrong estimate gets corrected next episode, once the agent tries it and sees the real reward. Offline there is no next episode: the overestimate becomes the target for the prior state's update too, compounding backward through the trajectory until a small overestimate becomes a policy confidently preferring an action nobody ever demonstrated.
Fixes split roughly into two camps: constrain the policy to stay close to what the data demonstrated (behavior-cloning-regularized methods, or support-matching approaches like BCQ), or constrain the value function to stay pessimistic on anything under-supported (CQL and related methods). This article uses the second family because it's simpler with a hand-written backprop loop — the correction adds straight into the loss, no second network needed, keeping the script under two hundred lines.
The architecture in this article is deliberately linear so the mechanism stays visible in the code rather than getting buried in framework abstractions:
Offline CQL pipeline, end to end
Fig. 1. The full offline pipeline: trade log and bar history become a transition dataset, the dataset trains a Q-network entirely offline, and only the resulting frozen weights ever reach the deployment EA.
Two things are worth noticing. First, no arrow feeds live ticks or Tester activity back into the training script —
CQL_OfflineTrain.mq5
is a
Script
, not an EA or indicator, and runs once, off-chart, against a static file. Second, the weights file is the only thing crossing from training to deployment: the EA never sees the raw dataset, only calling
Forward()
and
SelectAction()
on weights fixed before it started.
The CQL objective, in the form the code actually computes
The standard temporal-difference loss for a discrete-action Q-network is nothing unusual: fit
Q(s,a)
for the logged action toward the observed reward plus the discounted value of the best next action. What CQL adds is a second term, computed from the network's current output for every action at state
s
, not just the logged one:
L_TD(θ)    = 0.5 * ( Q_θ(s,a) - y )^2
y          = r + gamma * max_{a'} Q_θ(s', a') * (1 - done)

L_CQL(θ)   = alpha * ( logsumexp_{a} Q_θ(s,a) - Q_θ(s,a_data) )

L_total(θ) = L_TD(θ) + L_CQL(θ)
The
logsumexp_a
term is a smooth stand-in for "the value the current policy would extract by picking greedily" — dominated by whichever action has the highest Q-value, softened by the others in proportion to closeness. Subtracting
Q(s,a_data)
makes the penalty small when the logged action already dominates, large when an undemonstrated action is winning.
alpha
controls the strength: too small and extrapolation error creeps back, too large and the network grows too pessimistic to prefer any action.
Differentiating the CQL term with respect to each output
Q(s,a)
gives a clean, cheap gradient: exactly
softmax(Q(s,.))[a]
, with an extra
-1
subtracted at the logged action. That's the whole reason this is tractable to implement by hand in MQL5 — no behavior-cloning network, no importance sampling over actions, just a softmax over three numbers the forward pass already computed. The full
TrainStep()
implementation below computes this directly:
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| CQLQNetwork::TrainStep                                           |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
double
CQLQNetwork::TrainStep(
const
CQLTransition &batch[],
const
int
batch_size,
const
double
alpha,
const
double
gamma,
const
double
lr)
  {
//--- gradient accumulators, zeroed once per mini-batch (batch SGD).
//--- as in the constructor, fixed-size 2D arrays cannot be zeroed a row at
//--- a time via ArrayInitialize(), so each element is set explicitly
double
gW1[CQL_STATE_FEATURES][CQL_HIDDEN_UNITS];
double
gb1[CQL_HIDDEN_UNITS];
double
gW2[CQL_HIDDEN_UNITS][CQL_ACTION_COUNT];
double
gb2[CQL_ACTION_COUNT];
for
(
int
i =
0
; i < CQL_STATE_FEATURES; i++)
for
(
int
j =
0
; j < CQL_HIDDEN_UNITS; j++)
         gW1[i][j] =
0.0
;
for
(
int
j =
0
; j < CQL_HIDDEN_UNITS; j++)
for
(
int
a =
0
; a < CQL_ACTION_COUNT; a++)
         gW2[j][a] =
0.0
;
ArrayInitialize
(gb1,
0.0
);
ArrayInitialize
(gb2,
0.0
);
double
total_loss =
0.0
;
double
q_s[], q_next[];
for
(
int
n =
0
; n < batch_size; n++)
     {
//--- forward pass on s; m_pre/m_post are cached as a side effect and
//--- reused below for backprop through this same sample
Forward(batch[n].state, q_s);
double
hidden_cache[CQL_HIDDEN_UNITS];
double
pre_cache[CQL_HIDDEN_UNITS];
ArrayCopy
(hidden_cache, m_post);
//--- pre_cache must be copied now, before the second Forward() call
//--- below overwrites m_pre with next_state's pre-activations
ArrayCopy
(pre_cache, m_pre);
//--- bootstrapped TD target: r + gamma * max_a' Q(s',a') * (1-done).
//--- This is semi-gradient (no gradient flows through the target network,
//--- which here is just the same weights evaluated at s') - standard
//--- practice to keep training stable
Forward(batch[n].next_state, q_next);
double
max_next = q_next[
0
];
for
(
int
a =
1
; a < CQL_ACTION_COUNT; a++)
if
(q_next[a] > max_next)
            max_next = q_next[a];
double
target = batch[n].reward + (batch[n].done ?
0.0
: gamma * max_next);
int
a_logged = batch[n].action;
double
td_error  = q_s[a_logged] - target;
//--- CQL conservative term: softmax over the network's own current
//--- Q(s,.) approximates E_{a~mu}[Q(s,a)] via log-sum-exp; its gradient
//--- w.r.t. q_s[a] is softmax(q_s)[a], minus 1 at the logged action.
//--- This pushes down Q for actions the data never demonstrated while
//--- leaving the logged action's Q free to fit the TD target
double
max_q = q_s[
0
];
for
(
int
a =
1
; a < CQL_ACTION_COUNT; a++)
if
(q_s[a] > max_q)
            max_q = q_s[a];
double
exp_sum =
0.0
, softmax[CQL_ACTION_COUNT];
for
(
int
a =
0
; a < CQL_ACTION_COUNT; a++)
        {
         softmax[a] =
MathExp
(q_s[a] - max_q);
// subtract max_q for numerical stability
exp_sum   += softmax[a];
        }
for
(
int
a =
0
; a < CQL_ACTION_COUNT; a++)
         softmax[a] /= exp_sum;
double
log_sum_exp = max_q +
MathLog
(exp_sum);
      total_loss +=
0.5
* td_error * td_error + alpha * (log_sum_exp - q_s[a_logged]);
//--- combine TD gradient (only at the logged action) with the CQL
//--- penalty gradient (spread across every action via the softmax)
double
dLoss_dq[CQL_ACTION_COUNT];
for
(
int
a =
0
; a < CQL_ACTION_COUNT; a++)
         dLoss_dq[a] = alpha * softmax[a];
      dLoss_dq[a_logged] += td_error - alpha;
// TD term + CQL's -1 at the logged action
//--- backprop through the linear output layer: dL/dW2, dL/db2
double
dHidden[CQL_HIDDEN_UNITS];
ArrayInitialize
(dHidden,
0.0
);
for
(
int
a =
0
; a < CQL_ACTION_COUNT; a++)
        {
         gb2[a] += dLoss_dq[a];
for
(
int
j =
0
; j < CQL_HIDDEN_UNITS; j++)
           {
            gW2[j][a] += dLoss_dq[a] * hidden_cache[j];
            dHidden[j] += dLoss_dq[a] * m_W2[j][a];
// accumulate for layer 1
}
        }
//--- backprop through ReLU: gradient is zero wherever the pre-activation
//--- was <= 0 (the unit did not fire, so it contributed nothing forward)
for
(
int
j =
0
; j < CQL_HIDDEN_UNITS; j++)
        {
//--- pre_cache (this sample's s), not m_pre - by this point m_pre
//--- holds next_state's pre-activations from the Forward() call above
double
relu_grad = (pre_cache[j] >
0.0
) ? dHidden[j] :
0.0
;
         gb1[j] += relu_grad;
for
(
int
i =
0
; i < CQL_STATE_FEATURES; i++)
            gW1[i][j] += relu_grad * batch[n].state[i];
        }
     }
//--- apply averaged SGD update: mean gradient over the mini-batch keeps
//--- the effective learning rate independent of batch_size
double
inv_n =
1.0
/ batch_size;
for
(
int
i =
0
; i < CQL_STATE_FEATURES; i++)
for
(
int
j =
0
; j < CQL_HIDDEN_UNITS; j++)
         m_W1[i][j] -= lr * gW1[i][j] * inv_n;
for
(
int
j =
0
; j < CQL_HIDDEN_UNITS; j++)
      m_b1[j] -= lr * gb1[j] * inv_n;
for
(
int
j =
0
; j < CQL_HIDDEN_UNITS; j++)
for
(
int
a =
0
; a < CQL_ACTION_COUNT; a++)
         m_W2[j][a] -= lr * gW2[j][a] * inv_n;
for
(
int
a =
0
; a < CQL_ACTION_COUNT; a++)
      m_b2[a] -= lr * gb2[a] * inv_n;
return
(total_loss * inv_n);
  }
Reading it action by action: the TD half only touches the logged action's Q-value, exactly like ordinary Q-learning; the CQL half touches every action through the softmax, so
dLoss_dq[a_logged]
gets both the TD error and the CQL correction while every other action only gets the CQL push. From there it's standard backprop through a ReLU hidden layer, zeroed wherever
pre_cache[j] <= 0
.
pre_cache
matters because
Forward()
runs twice per sample (
state
, then
next_state
) and both overwrite the same
m_pre
/
m_post
buffers — reading
m_pre
afterward would mask the gradient with
next_state
's pre-activations; —
pre_cache
, copied right after the first call, keeps it correct.
One detail easy to miss: the CQL penalty here is computed against the network's own current Q-values at
s
, not a separate target network — unlike published CQL variants that keep one for the Bellman half, similar to DQN's trick. This keeps one weights file and no live/target synchronization, trading a little stability for simplicity; if a future dataset proves unstable, a target network is the first thing to add back, and the class is structured so a second, periodically-copied instance could be introduced without touching
Forward()
.
Training two networks on the same 838-transition dataset — one with
alpha=0
(CQL disabled), one with
alpha=1
(this article's default) — and comparing their Q-values where the rare action was never logged turns up an extreme case of CQL's failure mode:
FLAT
never appears once across all 838 transitions, since a trade log only records opens, making "do nothing" about as pure a case of an under-visited action as exists. This measures how far the CQL penalty moves a Q-value, not decision quality — a real improvement still needs evaluation on outcomes:
Naive Q-learning vs. CQL, measured on the actual dataset
Fig. 2. Mean Q-value for FLAT (0 of 838 transitions logged) and LONG (523 of 838 logged), averaged over the 315 states, drawn from the same training dataset, where the rare action was not what actually happened, comparing a network trained with alpha=0 against this article's alpha=1. FLAT's naive estimate sits near zero simply from having no gradient signal at all; CQL's penalty drives it sharply negative instead, actively discouraging an action the data gives no basis to trust. LONG, which is well-represented, also drops under CQL but by proportionally less, since its estimate is still anchored by real TD targets on every epoch.
The comparison in Fig. 2 was produced by
CQL_CompareAlpha.mq5
, a small standalone diagnostic script that is not part of the deployed system — it exists purely to measure what the CQL penalty is doing on this specific dataset, by loading two independently-trained networks and evaluating both on the same states:
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| OnStart                                                          |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
void
OnStart
(
void
)
  {
if
(!g_net_alpha0.LoadWeights(InpWeightsAlpha0))
     {
Print
(
"CQL_CompareAlpha: failed to load "
, InpWeightsAlpha0);
return
;
     }
if
(!g_net_alpha1.LoadWeights(InpWeightsAlpha1))
     {
Print
(
"CQL_CompareAlpha: failed to load "
, InpWeightsAlpha1);
return
;
     }
int
loaded = LoadDatasetForComparison(InpDatasetFile, g_dataset);
if
(loaded <=
0
)
     {
Print
(
"CQL_CompareAlpha: could not load dataset"
);
return
;
     }
//--- count how often each action appears in the logged data - the action
//--- with the fewest examples is the one naive Q-learning is most likely
//--- to overestimate, and the one CQL's penalty should visibly pull down
int
counts[CQL_ACTION_COUNT];
ArrayInitialize
(counts,
0
);
for
(
int
i =
0
; i < loaded; i++)
      counts[g_dataset[i].action]++;
int
rare_action =
0
;
for
(
int
a =
1
; a < CQL_ACTION_COUNT; a++)
if
(counts[a] < counts[rare_action])
         rare_action = a;
PrintFormat
(
"CQL_CompareAlpha: action counts - short=%d flat=%d long=%d (rarest = %d)"
,
               counts[CQL_ACTION_SHORT], counts[CQL_ACTION_FLAT], counts[CQL_ACTION_LONG], rare_action);
//--- average both networks' Q-value for the rare action, and separately for
//--- the most-logged action, ONLY over states where the rare action was NOT
//--- what actually happened - this is exactly the extrapolation scenario
//--- CQL is meant to guard against: judging an action the data barely tried
int
common_action =
0
;
for
(
int
a =
1
; a < CQL_ACTION_COUNT; a++)
if
(counts[a] > counts[common_action])
         common_action = a;
double
sum_rare0 =
0
, sum_rare1 =
0
, sum_common0 =
0
, sum_common1 =
0
;
int
n_eval =
0
;
double
q0[], q1[];
for
(
int
i =
0
; i < loaded; i++)
     {
if
(g_dataset[i].action == rare_action)
continue
;
// only evaluate on states where this action wasn't logged
g_net_alpha0.Forward(g_dataset[i].state, q0);
      g_net_alpha1.Forward(g_dataset[i].state, q1);
      sum_rare0   += q0[rare_action];
      sum_rare1   += q1[rare_action];
      sum_common0 += q0[common_action];
      sum_common1 += q1[common_action];
      n_eval++;
     }
PrintFormat
(
"CQL_CompareAlpha: over %d states (rare action=%d NOT logged):"
, n_eval, rare_action);
PrintFormat
(
"  rare action %d   -> alpha=0: %.4f   alpha=1: %.4f"
, rare_action, sum_rare0/n_eval, sum_rare1/n_eval);
PrintFormat
(
"  common action %d -> alpha=0: %.4f   alpha=1: %.4f"
, common_action, sum_common0/n_eval, sum_common1/n_eval);
  }
The script counts how often each action appears in the logged data, identifies the rarest and most common, then averages both networks' Q-value estimate for each — restricted to states where the rare action was
not
what actually happened, since that's precisely the extrapolation scenario CQL guards against. Running it is a one-time diagnostic: train a second set of weights with
alpha=0
under a different filename, run this script once, then discard that alpha=0 file — it never deploys.
Building the offline dataset from MQL5 trade logs
The dataset is nothing more exotic than rows of
(state, action, reward, next_state, done)
, but getting there from a real trade log takes care.
Export_TradeLog.mq5
reconstructs trades into
trade_log.csv
, and
Export_BarHistory.mq5
exports matching OHLC/ATR/RSI into
bar_history.csv
— both UTF-16, with a regional delimiter and a stray BOM.
build_offline_dataset.py
handles all three and walks both exports together to reconstruct the same feature vector the EA computes live, so training and deployment never see two definitions of "state":
def read_mql5_csv(path: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = pd.read_csv(path, encoding=
"utf-16"
, sep=None, engine=
"python"
)
    df.columns = df.columns.str.replace(
"﻿"
,
""
, regex=False)
return
df
On the MQL5 side,
LoadDataset()
reads back the plain UTF-8 CSV the Python script produces (deliberately not
FILE_CSV
's UTF-16, since training never round-trips through MetaTrader's export path). One wrinkle: it opens with
FILE_ANSI
, technically a different mode from UTF-8 — harmless here since every column is plain ASCII, but unsafe the moment a non-ASCII value enters one. It also grows its buffer geometrically instead of reading the file twice (once to count, once to load), which matters once a trade log spans years:
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| LoadDataset                                                      |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
int
LoadDataset(
const
string
filename, CQLTransition &dataset[])
  {
//--- offline_dataset.csv is written by build_offline_dataset.py using
//--- pandas' default UTF-8 (not FILE_CSV's native UTF-16), so this reads
//--- as a plain UTF-8 text file with a one-line header to skip
int
handle =
FileOpen
(filename,
FILE_READ
|
FILE_CSV
|
FILE_ANSI
|
FILE_COMMON
,
','
);
if
(handle ==
INVALID_HANDLE
)
     {
Print
(
"LoadDataset: cannot open "
, filename,
", err="
,
GetLastError
());
return
(-
1
);
     }
//--- header row: state_0..state_8,action,reward,next_state_0..next_state_8,done
for
(
int
c =
0
; c <
2
* CQL_STATE_FEATURES +
3
; c++)
FileReadString
(handle);
int
count =
0
;
ArrayResize
(dataset,
4096
);
// grown geometrically below as needed
while
(!
FileIsEnding
(handle))
     {
      CQLTransition row;
for
(
int
i =
0
; i < CQL_STATE_FEATURES; i++)
         row.state[i] =
StringToDouble
(
FileReadString
(handle));
      row.action = (
int
)
StringToInteger
(
FileReadString
(handle));
      row.reward =
StringToDouble
(
FileReadString
(handle));
for
(
int
i =
0
; i < CQL_STATE_FEATURES; i++)
         row.next_state[i] =
StringToDouble
(
FileReadString
(handle));
      row.done = (
StringToInteger
(
FileReadString
(handle)) !=
0
);
//--- all fields for this row are read regardless, so the file cursor
//--- stays aligned; only a malformed or out-of-range action is then
//--- dropped, rather than silently indexing Q-value arrays with it
if
(row.action <
0
|| row.action >= CQL_ACTION_COUNT)
continue
;
if
(count >=
ArraySize
(dataset))
ArrayResize
(dataset,
ArraySize
(dataset) *
2
);
      dataset[count++] = row;
     }
FileClose
(handle);
ArrayResize
(dataset, count);

(count);

Two design choices in
build_offline_dataset.py
deserve a word each. First,
reward
is taken directly from the trade log's realized profit column, with no shaping applied — a Sharpe-like or drawdown-penalized reward would encourage smoother equity curves, but changes what the Bellman target represents, and the CQL penalty's job only makes sense relative to whatever reward definition produced the data in the first place. Changing it later means rebuilding the dataset, not just retraining.
Worth flagging: the trade log and the deployment EA don't quite speak the same language. The log records completed trades — opened, closed — while deployment asks for a target exposure on every closed bar, so the dataset samples only the moments the logging strategy acted while the EA evaluates every bar. Reward attaches to a closed trade's P/L while the action in that row is the opening decision, making the chain a reasonable proxy for a bar-by-bar MDP, not an exact one.
The second is the
is_last_of_session
flag feeding the
done
column. Marking a transition terminal tells
TrainStep()
to drop the bootstrapped continuation term entirely (
batch[n].done? 0.0: gamma * max_next
), which matters at genuine boundaries — overnight gaps, a strategy change, an end-of-week flattening. treating every transition as non-terminal would inject a continuity assumption the market never promised.
The training loop, in
CQL_OfflineTrain.mq5
's
OnStart()
, is a script that never opens a chart connection to the live market. It loads the dataset once, computes the feature statistics the OOD guard will need later, shuffles before every epoch (otherwise a chronologically-ordered dataset biases each mini-batch toward whichever regime was active then), and calls
TrainStep()
per mini-batch:
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| OnStart                                                          |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
void
OnStart
(
void
)
  {
//--- Step 1: load the fixed offline dataset - this script never places
//--- a trade or reads a live tick; every transition below comes from a
//--- CSV a strategy or trade log already produced
int
loaded = LoadDataset(InpDatasetFile, g_dataset);
if
(loaded <=
0
)
     {
Print
(
"CQL_OfflineTrain: could not load dataset, aborting"
);
return
;
     }
Print
(
"CQL_OfflineTrain: loaded "
, loaded,
" transitions from "
, InpDatasetFile);
//--- Step 2: compute per-feature mean/stdev up front so the OOD guard
//--- ships baked into the same weights file as the policy it protects
ComputeFeatureStats(g_dataset, loaded, g_stats);
   g_network.SetFeatureStats(g_stats);
//--- Step 3: train
g_network.Init(InpRandomSeed);
MathSrand
(InpRandomSeed);
for
(
int
epoch =
0
; epoch < InpEpochs; epoch++)
     {
      ShuffleDataset(g_dataset, loaded);
// i.i.d. mini-batches, not chronological blocks
double
epoch_loss =
0.0
;
int
batches     =
0
;
//--- rows left over once loaded is not an exact multiple of InpBatchSize
//--- are simply not visited this epoch, rather than padded into a short
//--- final batch - a small, known gap in how much of the 838 rows each
//--- epoch actually uses
for
(
int

Twenty-four hidden units is a deliberately small choice, reached by starting smaller and increasing only until training loss stopped improving. A wider network isn't automatically better offline the way it might be online, where enough interaction fills capacity's blind spots — every added parameter is one more thing the fixed dataset must constrain, and an under-determined large network only worsens extrapolation error. Two layers is enough to fit the nine engineered features nonlinearly, with no library beyond MQL5's native arrays.
CQLQNetwork
is a plain two-layer feedforward net — nine inputs, twenty-four ReLU hidden units, three linear outputs.
Forward()
computes identically whether called from training or the deployment EA, removing one risk: the Q-value formula can't quietly diverge between the two. That guarantee stops at the feature vector feeding it, though —
build_offline_dataset.py
and
BuildStateVector()
are separate code computing the same state in two languages, kept aligned only by manual review; see "Feature drift" below.

Edge cases and pitfalls
Feature drift between training and deployment
. This is the single most common way an offline RL project silently fails after looking fine in training: if
BuildStateVector()
and
build_offline_dataset.py
ever compute a feature differently, the network evaluates live states against weights tuned for a distribution that never existed. The
CQL_STATE_FEATURES
check only catches a width mismatch, not a definition mismatch, so a change on one side needs the matching change on the other, by hand.
The OOD guard is a heuristic, not a proof
. A per-feature average z-score treats every feature as independently informative and misses correlated shifts — a state where every feature individually looks ordinary but the combination never occurred could still slip through. Averaging across all nine also means one wildly out-of-range feature can be masked if the other eight sit close to their means. Treat
CQL_OOD_MAX_ZSCORE
as a coarse tripwire worth calibrating against your own dataset's spread, not a guarantee.
The OOD guard fails open, not closed
.
IsOutOfDistribution()
returns
false
— in-distribution, safe to trade — whenever
m_stats_ready
is
false
, which happens if a weights file is loaded without its feature-statistics block. That choice favors keeping the EA trading over blocking it, the opposite of what "fail safe" usually means for a risk control: a missing or corrupted stats block disables the guard silently rather than disabling trading.
Alpha is not free to set once and forget
. Too low, and the conservative penalty stops doing meaningful work, letting extrapolation error back in. Too high, and every action's Q-value gets pulled toward the same conservative floor, making
SelectAction()
's argmax close to arbitrary among ties.
Reward design leaks into everything downstream
. This implementation uses raw realized trade P/L as the reward, deliberately unshaped. A shaped reward changes what the Bellman target represents and what the CQL penalty is conservative about — changing it after a dataset is built means rebuilding the dataset, not just retraining.
Inputs are not normalized before they reach the network
. The per-feature mean/stdev captured by
ComputeFeatureStats()
feed the OOD guard, but
Forwa

against: The trading signal uses future bar data: in BuildStateVector(), the code reads close_buf[5] and close_buf[4] (6- and 5-bar-back closes) to compute ret1 = (close_buf[5] - close_buf[4]) / close_buf[4], i.e., 1-bar return — but index 5 corresponds to a bar that closed 5 periods ago, and index 4 is 4 periods ago; however, the critical flaw is in the OnTick() logic: it triggers on iTime(_Symbol, PERIOD_CURRENT, 0) — the *current* (i.e., not-yet-closed) bar’s time — and then calls BuildStateVector(), which uses CopyClose(..., 0, 6, close_buf) to read the *last 6 closed bars*, i.e., indices 0–5 correspond to bars [now−1, now−2, ..., now−6]; thus ret1 = (close_buf[5] − close_buf[4]) / close_buf[4] computes return from bar now−6 to bar now−5 — fully historical. So this alone is not future-leak. However, the article explicitly warns: 'OnTick() triggers on the bar-time change and reads buffer index 0 for ATR, RSI, and close, which on most feeds is the bar that just opened, not the one that just finished' — and then says 'treat this as evaluating the newest available bar, not a guaranteed closed-bar read'. Crucially, BuildStateVector() uses atr_buf[0], rsi_buf[0], and close_buf[5] — but if index 0 of ATR/RSI buffers reflects the *still-open* current bar (as admitted), then atr_buf[0] and rsi_buf[0] are computed using incomplete price data (i.e., live tick stream within an open bar), meaning the state vector contains features derived from *intra-bar, non-closed, forward-looking* data — violating spot-Forex reproducibility, because spot brokers do not provide real-time ATR/RSI on open bars with deterministic, replayable values; these indicators are recalculated tick-by-tick and depend on unobservable intra-bar dynamics. This constitutes use of non-reproducible, effectively 'future' (relative to closed-bar context) data.

The rule cannot be written as a precise, self-contained formula because the article gives only a general architecture and implementation sketch without specifying the exact, deterministic conditions for entry/exit: while SelectAction() returns an action (LONG/SHORT/FLAT) based on argmax of Q-values, the actual trade execution logic in ApplyAction() is described as 'deliberately unambitious' and depends on runtime position state (e.g., 'close an opposing position first if one exists'), but the *exact timing and conditions under which the EA decides to act* are not fully specified as a standalone rule — e.g., OnTick() acts 'once per bar', but the bar detection relies on iTime(..., 0) whose behavior is broker-dependent and not guaranteed to align with closed-bar boundaries; the article admits 'shift to index 1 if your broker updates index 0 before the bar completes', confirming the condition is not deterministically defined across environments — thus the entry logic lacks a universal, formulaic specification independent of implementation quirks.

The method requires data unavailable in spot Forex: BuildStateVector() calls CopyTickVolume(_Symbol, PERIOD_CURRENT, 0, 3, volumes), which reads tick volume — a MetaTrader-specific proxy, not real traded volume; however, the article states 'spot-forex' excludes real volumes, and tick volume is not a true volume measure — but more critically, the OOD guard and feature engineering rely on ATR and RSI computed on the *current (open) bar* (as acknowledged: 'index 0 ... is the bar that just opened'), and such real-time indicator values on open bars are not standardized, not reproducible across brokers or backtest engines, and not part of the spot-forex data model — they require live tick stream processing with undefined latency and recalculation semantics, making them unavailable as deterministic inputs for spot-Forex strategy definition.
non_fatal: No mention of out-of-sample testing or train/test split — but per instructions, this is non-fatal.
No accounting for spread or commissions in reward calculation — non-fatal per instructions.
Reward is raw P/L without shaping — non-fatal, as it's consistent with offline dataset construction.
Alpha tuning is heuristic and dataset-dependent — non-fatal, as hyperparameter choice is part of validation.
Feature drift risk between Python and MQL5 implementations — non-fatal, as it's a maintainability issue, not a logical flaw in the rule itself.

judge.reject_reason: Фатальный порок: использование данных будущего в сигнале. В статье прямо указано, что OnTick() считывает индикаторы (ATR и RSI) по индексу 0, который «на большинстве фидов — это бар, который только что открылся, а не тот, что только что закрылся», и что «это оценка новейшего доступного бара, а не гарантированное чтение закрытого бара». При этом BuildStateVector() использует atr_buf[0] и rsi_buf[0], вычисленные на ещё незакрытом баре — то есть на данных, зависящих от внутрибарных тиков, которые недетерминированы, неповторяемы в спот-форексе, не доступны в закрытых барах и фактически представляют собой «будущие» (относительно закрытого бара) значения. Это нарушает требование детерминированного правила для проверки на закрытых барах.
judge.formula_and_logic: не применимо — правило не может быть записано как детерминированное условие входа, так как его входные данные (ATR[0], RSI[0]) зависят от незакрытого бара и не определены однозначно в контексте спот-форекса с закрытыми барами
judge.summary: Статья описывает реализацию Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) в MQL5 для офлайн-обучения торговой политики на исторических логах сделок без живого взаимодействия с рынком. Основной акцент сделан на подавлении экстраполяционной ошибки через штраф за действия, редко встречающиеся в обучающем датасете (например, FLAT — 0 из 838 переходов). Однако реализация зависит от значений индикаторов ATR и RSI, вычисляемых на текущем (незакрытом) баре, что делает сигнал недетерминированным и неприменимым для проверки на закрытых барах спот-форекса.
